records.title: Electricity Mid-Year Update 2026 — Executive summary
records.claim: Global electricity demand reached 28,600 TWh in 2025, up 3%; renewables supplied 33% of generation. In the first half of 2026, South Australia and California recorded negative wholesale prices in roughly 20% of hours. Flexibility faces technical, regulatory and contractual barriers.
records.period: 2025 annual estimates; observed first-half 2026 wholesale pricing. 2026–2027 full-year figures are forecasts.
records.locator: Executive summary: global demand, generation mix, wholesale prices and flexibility; report overview publication date.
records.region: Global for demand/generation; South Australia and California for negative-price frequency.

records.definition: Electricity generation is energy output, distinct from installed capacity. Negative-price frequency counts wholesale-market hours in specified regions.

records.title: Lithium-Ion Battery Pack Prices Fall to $108 Per Kilowatt-Hour Despite Rising Metal Prices: BloombergNEF
records.claim: BNEF’s 2025 survey estimated average lithium-ion pack prices at USD 108/kWh, down 8%; stationary-storage packs at 70, down 45%; BEV packs at 99. China averaged 84; North America and Europe were 44% and 56% higher respectively.
records.period: 2025 survey; year-on-year comparison with the survey’s 2024 baseline.
records.locator: Public release body: global average; stationary-storage and BEV packs; regional prices; survey explanation.

records.title: Renewable power generation costs in 2025
records.claim: 2025 global weighted-average LCOE: solar PV USD 44/MWh, onshore wind 33, offshore wind 78. Since 2010, these fell 89%, 71% and 63%. Four-hour utility-scale BESS installed cost averaged USD 140/kWh. Four-hour turnkey cost averaged 111/kWh, excluding EPC, grid connection and development.
records.published: July 2026; verified to month precision through PNNL's institutional catalogue. Exact original release day not independently verified.
records.period: Projects commissioned in 2025; historical comparison with 2010; 2025 storage cost estimates.
records.locator: Executive summary, printed/PDF pp11–16; Table 1.1, pp14–15; regional comparisons, p16; exclusion-of-China comparison, p23; battery storage, pp139–144; four-hour turnkey definition and cost, p143.; solar scope: p.70, section 3.6 and footnote 17
records.region: Global cost averages; explicitly separate selected country samples.
records.unit: 2025 USD/MWh for LCOE; 2025 USD/kWh for BESS equipment and installed costs; percent.
records.definition: LCOE is a lifetime generation cost metric. Installed BESS, turnkey equipment and battery packs have different cost boundaries. The solar PV benchmark covers standalone utility-scale projects; rooftop PV is outside it.
records.type: Original IRENA cost study; storage estimates incorporate third-party BloombergNEF data.
records.method: Use reported weighted averages; no pack-to-system subtraction or direct inference about project selling prices. Cutoff verification: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Tethys Engineering catalogue, https://tethys-engineering.pnnl.gov/publications/renewable-power-generation-costs-2025.
records.limit: LCOE does not include the same services as firm electricity. Cost averages do not establish company margins. USD 240/kWh in the selected-market component chart is not the global USD 140/kWh benchmark. Raw survey observations were not separately audited.
records.redistribution: Link to the publisher; no original research file is included in the review package.

records.title: Energy Technology Perspectives 2026 — Supply chain risks and industrial competitiveness
records.claim: In 2024, China held about 85% of solar PV and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply-chain capacity on a value-weighted basis excluding mining. Each examined technology had an upstream bottleneck outside China. Manufacturing efficiency explained over 40% of the modelled Europe–China battery cost gap.
records.period: 2024 supply-chain baseline and cost model; conditional future scenarios are separate.
records.locator: Supply chain risks and industrial competitiveness: concentration chart and notes; N−1 supply-chain analysis and notes; Manufacturing efficiency and battery production costs. Publication date: report overview.
records.region: Global manufacturing stages; China, Europe and the rest of the world.
records.unit: Percent of value-weighted capacity; percent of modelled cost differences.
records.definition: Concentration is value-weighted across manufacturing stages, excluding extraction; N−1 removes the largest supplying country under stated assumptions.
records.type: Original IEA synthesis and scenario/cost modelling using third-party datasets.
records.method: N−1 assumes 85% nameplate utilisation for manufacturing; mineral stages use actual production. Battery comparison models NMC811/graphite.
records.limit: These are 2024 capacity/model results, not 2026 shipments, headquarters shares, contracts or actual disruption losses. Non-Chinese downstream capacity alone does not demonstrate an independent supply chain. A modelled cost gap cannot establish company profitability.
records.redistribution: Link to the publisher; no original research file is included in the review package.

records.title: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 — Executive summary

The largest refining country’s average share, excluding rare earths, rose to 72% from 70% in 2023. New refining projects outside incumbents face higher costs and equipment, technology and skills constraints.

records.region: Global critical-mineral markets; leading refining country varies by mineral.
records.unit: Year-on-year percent investment changes; average leading-country refining share.
records.definition: Refining concentration is the leading single country’s average share across the specified minerals, excluding rare earths.

records.title: 24/7 renewables: The economics of firm solar and wind
records.claim: A hypothetical 100 MW Las Vegas solar case uses 2025 costs. At a 95% energy-coverage target, solar plus storage and overbuild costs USD 113.2/MWh versus 43.5 standalone, with 591.8 MWh of storage and 61.9 MW of additional solar.
records.published: Publicly catalogued by 20 May 2026; KETEP registration date verified. The original publisher's first release date remains unverified.
records.event: Not applicable: model illustration, not a constructed project or contract.
records.period: Hypothetical reference case using 2025 cost assumptions; selected-project analysis uses 2024 commissioned projects.
records.locator: Firm LCOE definition, printed/PDF pp8–9 and p24; Las Vegas illustration, pp25–26; Table 1, p26.
records.region: Hypothetical Las Vegas, United States reference case; selected global project samples elsewhere.
records.unit: USD/MWh; MW solar capacity; MWh battery capacity; percent of annual demand energy.
records.definition: Firm LCOE adds a firming premium. Reliability here means energy coverage of flat annual demand, not system adequacy.
records.type: Original IRENA model analysis and illustrative scenario.
records.method: Model uses flat hourly demand; 43.5 + 69.7 = 113.2 USD/MWh. Cutoff verification: Korea Institute of Energy Technology Evaluation and Planning, Global Energy catalogue, https://energy.ketep.re.kr/globalenergy/site/main/board/policy_report/31728.
records.limit: The 95% target does not mean uninterrupted supply at every hour or guaranteed peak capacity. Results are location-specific model outputs, not project invoices, average market prices, actual orders or storage returns. Future cost trajectories are conditional projections.
records.redistribution: Link to the publisher; no original research file is included in the review package.
